strengths: The core idea is simple, elegant, and practically appealing: modifying the attention mask so image tokens can attend to text tokens (MMA) requires no additional parameters, no extra training time, and is trivially compatible with existing MLLM training pipelines, unlike prior data-centric or connector-based solutions.

The paper provides a thorough set of controlled ablations (Table 1) under identical data/training configurations comparing the standard causal pipeline, a strong state-of-the-art baseline (CCA), an intuitive dual-order training (DOT) alternative with four sub-variants, and the proposed MMA, which helps isolate the effect of the architectural change from confounds like data scale.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation across 12 benchmarks spanning general, knowledge, and vision-centric categories, with detailed per-category breakdowns in the appendix (Tables 7-15) that aid interpretability and reproducibility.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, dataset statistics, and stated intent to release code and the AKI-4B model.

The scaled-up AKI-4B model shows competitive or superior performance versus several 3B/7B open-source and proprietary baselines despite using substantially less pretraining data/lower resolution, suggesting the architectural change may be a genuinely useful lever independent of data scale.
Honest limitations section acknowledging that MMA is only applied at SFT (not PT) due to information-leakage concerns, rather than overselling generality.
weaknesses: The method is evaluated only at a single, relatively small model scale (4B parameters, Phi-3.5-mini backbone) and only for image-text pairs; the claimed generality to "other modalities" and "interleaved multimodal data" (Eq. 6, broader impacts) is purely speculative and untested, which somewhat overstates the scope of the contribution.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported; some benchmark deltas are small (e.g., POPE +1%, CV-Bench3D +2.1%) or come from benchmarks with limited sample sizes (e.g., MME cognition split), making it hard to assess whether gains are robust or within noise.

The technical novelty is incremental: the change is a targeted attention-mask modification closely related to prior work (CCA), and the paper's framing as a "fundamental" architectural fix is somewhat oversold relative to the modest scope of the actual modification (unlocking image-to-question-text attention only in SFT).

Table 2 comparisons mix models trained with very different data scale, resolution, and vision-token counts (e.g., 6.7B vs 1.4T pretraining tokens), which the paper acknowledges but which still makes it difficult to cleanly attribute AKI-4B's competitive results to the MMA mechanism itself versus other design choices (OCR data, resampler, etc.); an ablation isolating MMA's effect at the AKI-4B scale (i.e., AKI-4B with vs without MMA) would strengthen the causal claim substantially and is notably absent.
AKI-4B substantially underperforms peer models on knowledge-heavy benchmarks (MMMU, MathVista), which limits the paper's claim of broad, general improvement in multimodal understanding.

The restriction of MMA to the SFT stage (with PT left as future work due to leakage issues) is a nontrivial limitation that constrains the method's applicability to the standard two-stage pipeline and leaves open how the technique would interact with more modern single-stage or continually pretrained MLLM regimes.

Qualitative results (Appendix D) are a small, cherry-picked set of anecdotal examples rather than systematic human evaluation of hallucination reduction, limiting the strength of the object-hallucination narrative beyond the POPE numbers.

strengths: Identifies a clear, well-motivated architectural limitation (causal attention preventing earlier modality tokens from attending to later modality/text tokens) and proposes a simple, parameter-free, training-cost-free fix (MMA) that is easy to integrate into existing MLLM pipelines.

Rigorous, apples-to-apples ablation study (Table 1) comparing the conventional I&T pipeline, the state-of-the-art CCA baseline, the intuitive dual-order training (DOT) approach and several DOT ablations, all trained with identical data/configurations, which convincingly isolates the effect of the proposed attention modification.
Broad evaluation across 12 benchmarks spanning general, knowledge, and vision-centric categories, with consistent gains (11/12 benchmarks) over CCA and other baselines.

AKI-4B achieves competitive or superior results versus larger 7B and similarly-sized 3-4B open/proprietary models despite substantially less pretraining data/lower resolution, suggesting the architectural change is a meaningful and efficient lever.
Strong reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, dataset composition, and per-category benchmark breakdowns are all provided in the appendix.
Honest and specific limitation discussion (MMA benefits confined to SFT stage due to information-leakage in PT), rather than generic boilerplate limitations.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is essentially a targeted change to the attention mask; while effective and simple, the method offers limited architectural or theoretical novelty beyond CCA and related masking tricks, and the paper provides largely empirical rather than mechanistic justification for why this specific unlocking helps.

The claimed generality to interleaved multimodal or multi-modality (e.g., audio) scenarios (Eq. 6, Broader Impacts) is not empirically validated anywhere in the paper — only single image-text pairs are tested, making the generalization claims speculative.

The information-leakage constraint restricting MMA to the SFT stage only is a substantive limitation that undercuts the claim of a fully generic, stage-agnostic solution; no mitigation or partial fix is attempted.

Experiments are limited to a single relatively small model scale (4B, Phi-3.5-mini backbone); no evidence is given that gains persist or scale favorably at larger LLM sizes, which is important given the trend toward larger MLLMs.
Results appear to be single-run (no seeds/variance reported), so the statistical robustness of reported improvements (some benchmarks show small margins, e.g., POPE +1%) is unclear.
Qualitative analysis (Appendix D) is based on only 4 cherry-picked examples and does not constitute a systematic qualitative/error analysis of hallucination reduction.

Comparison fairness to SOTA 7B/3B models (Table 2) is compromised by differing training data scale, resolution, and vision token count, which the authors acknowledge but which still limits the strength of claims about AKI-4B's superiority.
Minor presentation issues remain (e.g., an apparent formatting error in Table 8, '0.65' for RR under AKI-4B, which is inconsistent with the percentage scale used elsewhere).
